old_entry.title: ZX Spectrum
old_entry.subtitle: A keyboard, a cassette and a new possibility
old_entry.summary: An affordable British microcomputer helped make playing and programming neighbours.
body: Sinclair's ZX Spectrum arrived in 1982. Its compact keyboard and cassette-based software placed a programmable computer within reach of many British households. Games could come from a shop, a magazine listing or someone experimenting at home.

Its characteristic colour attributes became part of a recognisable graphic style. The wider home-computer scene also supported small publishers and designers whose work did not need to begin inside a console manufacturer.

editorial_features.title: A cassette leaves the bedroom
body: Steve Wetherill remembered learning to program in an unheated Barnsley bedroom. His mother had bought him a Spectrum and a small television; a cassette held the assembler he needed to write code. A crash could mean rewinding and loading it again. Borrowing the family's colour set meant competing with everyone else's viewing. In his account, the route into games passed through ordinary domestic arrangements: money found for a machine, space borrowed from a household and evenings spent waiting for a tape to finish.

A demonstration could travel where its maker had never worked. Wetherill recalled answering magazine advertisements by posting a cassette protected between pieces of cardboard. His scrolling platformer secured an interview at Software Projects in Liverpool in early 1984. Another candidate was Stoo Fotheringham, who later moved from programming into pixel art. Wetherill's account follows that meeting into shared accommodation and offices in a former hosiery factory. The bedroom was a starting place; a postal package opened the way to colleagues, employers and another city.

Bob Pape's demonstration tape carried a rejected idea as well as a job application. He had made additions to The Quill adventure system, including text compression and scrolling, but its makers were uninterested. He put those experiments alongside other work and sent them to Catalyst Coders. The tape helped him obtain the Rampage commission. Remembering it in 1997, Pape described a practical portfolio assembled from things he had already tried. An unsuccessful approach to one company became evidence of useful skills for another.

Pape remembered making Spectrum R-Type alongside programmers handling other versions in a Fareham office. Its colour also depended on a technical choice: characters moved in steps while the background scrolled by pixels. He credited Mark Jones's graphics and Rob Hylands's sound driver elsewhere in the interview. The conversion brought together distinct kinds of knowledge about the same small machine. Behind the image of the solitary bedroom programmer stood artists, specialists and fellow developers, sharing the work that turned an arcade game into a home version.
